A publicly traded North American banking and financial services institution operating across a broad geographic footprint with a large, distributed workforce. Its scale and regulatory environment require consistent identity governance across a complex stack, including enterprise IGA, PAM, and ITSM systems.
The financial institution had invested in enterprise identity governance tools to manage access at scale, but when it came to Completeness and Accuracy (C&A), it wasn’t enough.
. C&A is not a platform problem. It is an execution problem. That is the gap Alex was hired to close.

Most of every cycle was spent following up with application owners to produce the evidence auditors required. Manual nudges, repeated escalations, and re-requests consumed analyst capacity and delayed remediation.
Endless follow-up → Scheduled Process Kickoff.
Alex kicks off each cycle, runs the heavy lifting end-to-end (data preparation, evidence collection, scope checks, quality review), and brings a human in only to confirm and certify.

Alex communicates with end users and application owners directly in Microsoft Teams, nudges, escalates, and explains entitlements with business context so reviewers approve because they understand, not because they are tired.
Every action carried a reasoned, logged audit trail. Alex’s outputs gave the IAM team better evidence than they could produce manually.

Automating Epic Onboarding and Provisioning
Epic Onboarding at Wire Speed
Alex maps every new hire to the right Epic template overnight, so the access decision is made before the team starts its day.
Integration projects required
The bottleneck was never writing access into Epic. It was deciding which template each new hire should receive.
Alex is deliberately not connected to Epic. He hands over a reviewable file, so no integration project was needed.
A human approves every grant, which is what keeps over-provisioning of protected health records out of the process.

In a health system, almost everyone needs Epic access before they can do their job, and getting it right matters in three directions at once. It is critical: a clinician waiting on access cannot see patients or chart. It is high-volume: every new hire needs it, continuously. And it must be precise: each person should see exactly what their role requires, and nothing more.

Epic makes access precise through a permission model of templates and sub templates. The hard part is deciding which template each new hire should get, based on department, site, the specific hospital, and role. At the health system, that decision was manual: one onboarding ticket at a time, done by hand.
For every ticket, an expert gathered a new hire’s attributes and searched the template register by hand to find the right match.
The rules were clear and the expertise was there. The limit was how much judgment-heavy work one team can do by hand as new hires keep arriving.
Delays in provisioning meant clinicians could be left unable to see patients or chart on day one.
Precision under regulation:
Over-provisioning a single grant risks exposing protected health records. Every mapping has to be exactly right.

Recertifying meant managers logging into 13 acquired banners’ legacy portals, so large owners approved on autopilot.
A national retailer operating more than 2,000 stores across 30-plus states under 13 regional brands assembled over a decade of acquisitions.

Retail runs on people who do not work for you. Vendor merchandisers set the displays, equipment and facilities techs keep the stores running, cleaning crews come in overnight, and distribution-center temps carry the holiday peak. At this retailer there are roughly 23,000 of them, one contractor for every five associates.
Acquisitions multiplied the friction.

The retailer already owned a governance suite and had built its own weekly-renewal portal. Both were part of the problem: the suite struggled with custom and long-tail apps, and the homegrown portal forced cross-banner logins and was slated for sunset.
Alex correlates accounts across the 13 acquired banners’ directories to surface orphaned and duplicate access ahead of the identity migration.
Learn how a Fortune 500 bank used Twine’s AI Digital Employee, Alex, to transform its Completeness and Accuracy program and close critical identity governance gaps.
Alex ran the collection work end to end: opening a Teams conversation with each named owner, validating answers as they arrived, and escalating to a manager when an owner went quiet.

Onboarding an application to the governance platform starts with a template: what the application is, what risk tier it belongs to, what entitlements it carries, and what each of those entitlements actually means. No system in the stack holds that answer.

The template goes out and nothing comes back. Someone follows up, then follows up again. Answers arrive partial, and the clarifying questions start a second round. The whole thing rests on one person’s persistence, and that person’s actual job is running the identity program.
An account correlated to a person loses its owner when that person leaves. Application-local accounts cannot even be listed without asking every owner what they have.
Alex checks answers as they arrive and re-asks what is missing, rather than accepting an incomplete form and handing the gap back to the identity team.
The bank’s security team never asked whether to allow this. It asked how tightly it could be bounded. Four answers carried the review.
